title: Vessel Diameter and Flow
question: How do tube diameter and driving pressure affect the amount of fluid that flows each minute?

blocks.prompt: Required before collecting: Predict how a wider tube could affect flow at the same pressure difference. Separately, predict what doubling pressure difference could do in the original tube. Give reasons.
blocks.text: A wider bore may allow more flow at fixed pressure; doubling pressure may also increase rate. These are different controlled changes, not a narrow-faster rule for every experiment.

blocks.prompt: Required before collecting: What should stay fixed in a diameter comparison? Why return to the original diameter to test pressure? Explain how three different conditions differ from three repeated trials.
blocks.text: Match10cm length, fixed viscosity/model fluid and5model-minute interval. Baseline2mm/1×pressure; diameter4mm/1×; pressure2mm/2×. These three conditions isolate two variables with a shared baseline and do not measure independent biological variation.
Timing: Before assembly or any model collection.

Diameter alone changes2→4mm at1×pressure; pressure alone1→2× uses the original2mm tube. Same10cm length/fixed viscosity/fluid/time and ideal regulator. Doubling diameter doubles radius: chosen laminar flow scales with radius⁴ and pressure factor, so2⁴=16 versus a linear pressure factor2. Opening area4× and flow16× imply average speed4× since Q=area×speed. Narrower-faster continuity assumes the same flow, which is not fixed here. Distinguish flow rate from speed and explain the limits of a single ideal tube for blood vessels.

blocks.prompt: At fixed pressure, doubling a circular tube’s diameter doubles its radius too. In this laminar model, what happens to flow?
blocks.text:
It becomes sixteen times as large; the radius acts to the fourth power.
Correct! The ideal law includes radius four times in a product.2×2×2×2=16. Both area and the velocity profile change under a fixed pressure difference. Correct on first recorded check.

blocks.prompt: The wider tube has four times the area and sixteen times the flow here. What happens to its average speed?
blocks.text:
It is four times as large: flow ÷ area gives average speed.
Correct! Flow rate = area × average speed. The ratio16÷4=4 applies here. The common narrower-faster claim assumes the same flow, which was not fixed in this comparison. Revised after feedback.

blocks.prompt: Can these three ideal collections give a person’s blood pressure or diagnose a circulation problem?
blocks.text:
No. Real blood, changing vessel walls, pulses and networks need more evidence.
Correct! These are controlled model outputs. Repetition cannot turn a simplified chosen model into a clinical measurement. Correct on first recorded check.

Chosen inputs and a reference rate generate these volumes; they are not physical blood, pressure or viscosity measurements. Assume smooth layered flow of a fluid that hardly compresses and has fixed viscosity. The long, rigid round tube has no branches, pulses, blood cells or moving walls. Turbulence and body regulation are omitted. An ideal replenished source holds driving pressure difference steady across the test tube, including height effects. Start/stop changes and connector losses are ignored. Bores are enlarged; width and length do not share a scale. Five minutes is model time. One collection per condition cannot show variation or a population effect. Real vessels change radius through smooth muscle and form networks. This model cannot predict a person’s pressure, flow, health or treatment. Flow rate is volume per time; speed is distance per time. A narrower section can be faster when the same flow passes through it. Here pressure, rather than flow, stays fixed in the diameter comparison.
